body: NIST DLMF section 27.11 (Asymptotic Formulas: Partial Sums) says: "The behavior of a number-theoretic function f(n) for large n is often difficult to determine because the function values can fluctuate considerably as n increases. It is more fruitful to study partial sums and seek asymptotic formulas of the form where F(x) is a known function of x , and O\left(g(x)\right) represents the error, a function of smaller order than F(x) for all x in some prescribed range. For example, Dirichlet ( 1849 ) proves that for all x\geq 1 , where \gamma is Euler’s constant (§ 5.2(ii) ). Dirichlet’s divisor problem (unsolved as of 2022) is to determine the least number \theta_{0} such that the error term in ( 27.11.2 ) is O\left(x^{\theta}\right) for all \theta>\theta_{0} . Huxley ( 2003 ) proves that \theta_{0}\leq\frac{131}{416} . Equations ( 27.11.3 )–( 27.11.11 ) list further asymptotic formulas related to some of the functions listed in § 27.2 . They are valid for all x\geq 2 . The error terms given here are not necessarily the best known." Equation 27.11.1 on the page has alt text "\sum_{n\leq x}f(n)=F(x)+O\left(g(x)\right),". Equation 27.11.2 on the page has alt text "\sum_{n\leq x}d\left(n\right)=x\ln x+(2\gamma-1)x+O\left(\sqrt{x}\right),". This card records that section's wording and equation alt text. It does not retypeset a formula the alt text did not carry.
